Equivalence becomes a finite calculation, which we mechanize in Agda for a fragment and use to prove the VHamilton form of the compiler rewrite "rzz(t) = cx; rz(t); cx" for every clock value. We then show what the same structure supports in a two-qubit chemistry eigensolver written in VHamilton and run through a Haskell prototype. It supports a fusion of commuting blocks, a closed form and an expressibility proof for the ansatz, and an exact split of the error between the precision of the target and that of the clocks, with a priori bounds. It also supports a coordinate search whose queries per sweep, fixed by the spectra of the generators, do not grow with the precision. On the benchmark this search reaches the numerically verified optimum of a grid of 134 million valuations in 53 energy queries. It finds the grid optimum in only 21 of 30 validation settings, however, so the gain is conditional, not a global-optimization guarantee.
tldr: VHamilton extends the Hamilton quantum programming language with open clocks so that variational Hamiltonian evolution durations can be treated symbolically, verified in Agda, and optimized for a two-qubit chemistry eigensolver.
motivation: Variational quantum algorithms require a classical optimizer to choose evolution durations, but standard circuit-level programming loses the Hamiltonian structure needed to reason about all parameter valuations at once.
method: The authors define variational programs as families of Hamiltonian trajectories with open clocks filled by exact dyadic times, keep the semantics exact and affine in clocks, mechanize equivalence checking in Agda for a fragment, and implement a Haskell prototype for a two-qubit chemistry eigensolver with block fusion and coordinate search.
result: They prove the compiler rewrite rzz(t) = cx; rz(t); cx for all clock values, obtain a closed form and expressibility proof for the ansatz, split error between target precision and clock precision with a priori bounds, and reach the numerical optimum of a 134-million-point grid in 53 energy queries on the benchmark, though only in 21 of 30 validation settings.
conclusion: Open-clock variational programs enable exact symbolic reasoning and query-efficient search, but the speedup is conditional rather than a global-optimization guarantee.

title: Electronic-Structure-Informed Many-Body Encoding For Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Liangnuo Zhang, Tanner Culpitt, Qiwei Yin, Linghua Zhu, Xiaosong Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data encoding is a central challenge in quantum machine learning (QML), as it determines how classical information is mapped onto quantum states and influences the expressive power and efficiency of parameterized quantum circuits. Here, we introduce a physics-informed quantum encoding strategy that exploits the intrinsic many-body structure of electronic systems to establish a direct correspondence between the body order of input descriptors and the locality of quantum gates. Specifically, [MATH]-body electronic descriptors obtained from a single mean-field electronic-structure calculation are encoded through [MATH]-qubit gates, yielding a systematic hierarchy of quantum circuits with increasing many-body expressivity. Using reduced-density-matrix descriptors, we construct quantum machine-learning models incorporating one- through four-body encodings and benchmark their performance in predicting electron-correlation energies along bond-stretching potential energy surfaces. We demonstrate that increasing the body order of the encoding systematically improves prediction accuracy toward the full configuration interaction limit. Remarkably, disconnected many-particle densities constructed from lower-order electronic information achieve accuracy comparable to explicitly correlated two-particle densities in key cases, providing a computationally inexpensive route to higher-body quantum encodings. These findings establish a connection between the many-body structure of classical data and the design of quantum feature maps, offering a systematic, physically interpretable framework for enhancing the expressivity and predictive performance of quantum machine-learning circuits.
tldr: The authors propose a physics-informed data-encoding strategy for quantum machine learning in which k-body electronic-structure descriptors are mapped onto k-qubit gates, producing a hierarchy of circuit ansätze whose many-body expressivity can be systematically increased.
motivation: Data encoding is a bottleneck in QML because it fixes how classical information enters a quantum state and thus bounds the expressivity and efficiency of parameterized circuits; the authors seek an encoding that is physically interpretable and grounded in the actual many-body structure of the input data.
method: Reduced-density-matrix descriptors from a single mean-field electronic-structure calculation are used to build one-, two-, three- and four-body encodings implemented via multi-qubit gates, and the resulting QML models are benchmarked on predicting electron-correlation energies along bond-stretching potential energy surfaces.
result: Increasing the body order of the encoding systematically improves prediction accuracy toward the full-configuration-interaction limit, and disconnected many-particle densities built from lower-order information match explicitly correlated two-particle densities in key cases.
conclusion: The work links the many-body structure of classical chemical data to quantum feature-map design, offering a physically interpretable and computationally cheaper route to higher-body quantum encodings for chemical QML.

title: Characteristics Of Vhf And Uhf Band Detection Using Stark Shifting In Rydberg-atom Sensors
authors: Rajavardhan Talashila, Noah Schlossberger, David S. la Mantia, Abby Halasi-Kun, Baran Kayim, Michael A. Viray, Robert Wyllie, Christopher L. Holloway, Nikunjkumar Prajapati
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a characterization of the sensitivity of broadband electric field measurements in the Very High Frequency (VHF) and Ultra High Frequency (UHF) bands using AC stark shifting of Rydberg states. The dependence of the sensitivity and dynamic range of the field measurements using nD5/2 states of cesium for principal quantum numbers n= 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100 is presented, detailing the intricacies involved. The frequencies considered for the measurement range from 50 MHz to 900 MHz for which a transverse electromagnetic (TEM) cell is used to excite the Rydberg atoms with the RF fields. The corresponding sensitivities achieved are in the [MATH] range. A general trend of better sensitivity for higher principal quantum numbers is observed. This work paves the way for a better understanding of the AC Stark dependent field measurements using Rydberg sensors.
tldr: Characterizes the sensitivity and dynamic range of broadband VHF/UHF electric-field sensing via AC Stark shifting of cesium nD5/2 Rydberg states for principal quantum numbers 60–100.
motivation: Rydberg-atom sensors offer calibrated, traceable electric-field metrology, but their sensitivity and dynamic range in the VHF/UHF bands via AC Stark shift readout are not well characterized across principal quantum numbers.
method: Cesium atoms in nD5/2 Rydberg states (n = 60, 70, 80, 90, 100) are excited by RF fields from 50 MHz to 900 MHz in a transverse electromagnetic (TEM) cell, and the resulting AC Stark shift response is used to extract sensitivity and dynamic range.
result: Sensitivities in the mV/cm range are achieved, with a general trend of improved sensitivity at higher principal quantum numbers, alongside a mapping of the trade-offs and intricacies across the studied band.
conclusion: The work provides a systematic characterization of AC-Stark-based Rydberg field sensing in the VHF/UHF regime, supporting design choices for broadband Rydberg receivers rather than advancing quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Learning Finite-Memory Binary Sources
authors: Maciej Skorski
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Estimating biased finite-memory sources from a single trajectory is a fundamental problem with practical impact, for example in estimating entropy for cryptography. We study order-[MATH] binary sources whose conditional probabilities have bias at most [MATH], and establish *sharp* sample complexity bounds: relative accuracy [MATH] with confidence [MATH] needs [MATH] samples up to constants depending on [MATH], with matching upper and lower bounds and no dependence on mixing time or spectral gap. The proof rests on a sharp bound on expected hitting times of the sliding-window (de Bruijn) chain, which stay of order [MATH] uniformly in [MATH] exactly when [MATH], and on majorization of the window masses by those of independent biased coins. Applied to published entropy-source validations, the bounds show that their trace lengths may be underpowered: [MATH] bits cannot resolve all transitions of an [MATH]-bit model to better than about [MATH] relative error.
tldr: This paper derives sharp sample-complexity bounds for learning finite-memory binary sources and estimating their entropy from a single trajectory.
motivation: Estimating biased finite-memory sources is important for cryptographic entropy validation, but existing trace-length requirements may be underpowered.
method: The author studies order-M binary sources with bounded conditional bias and proves matching upper and lower sample-complexity bounds using expected hitting times of the sliding-window de Bruijn chain and majorization arguments.
result: The bounds show that relative accuracy with high confidence requires a number of samples independent of mixing time or spectral gap, and published entropy-source validations may be underpowered.
conclusion: The work provides a classical information-theoretic analysis of source estimation with implications for entropy validation in cryptography, but it does not address quantum information or quantum cryptographic protocols.

title: Privacy-Constrained Function Computation In Distributed Databases
authors: R\'emi A. Chou Vamoua Yachongka
abstract: ArXiv:2610.41034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Consider distributed databases that contain both sensitive (private) and non-sensitive (public) attributes. A user seeks to compute a function of public attributes and side information by interacting with the databases and downloading their responses. In this paper, we study the trade-offs among download cost, information leakage about the private attributes, and distortion between the computed function and its reconstruction, referred to as the capacity region. Our main contributions are as follows. For a single database, we provide a complete characterization of the capacity region for general discrete sources and characterize the capacity region of two different setups for Gaussian sources when the computed function is defined as the sum of the public attribute and side information. For distributed databases, we establish inner and outer bounds on the capacity region of discrete sources and we characterize the capacity region when the databases and the side information are mutually independent. As a special instance, we study lossless function computation, and results analogous to the lossy case are obtained.
tldr: The paper characterizes trade-offs among download cost, private-attribute information leakage, and function reconstruction distortion for privacy-constrained function computation over distributed databases.
motivation: Distributed databases often mix sensitive private attributes with public data, so computing functions without leaking private information requires understanding fundamental information-theoretic limits.
method: The authors derive capacity regions for single-database discrete and Gaussian sources, and inner/outer bounds for distributed databases, including exact characterization under independence assumptions.
result: They provide complete characterizations for single-database general discrete sources and two Gaussian setups for sum functions, plus bounds and an exact distributed-database characterization for mutually independent databases and side information, with lossless computation as a special case.
conclusion: The work establishes information-theoretic limits for privacy-constrained function computation in distributed databases, but it is classical and does not involve quantum information.

title: Intensity-Domain Demultiplexing Of Orbital Angular Momentum Channels For Optical Communication
authors: Junsu Kim, Jiwon Jung, Hyunchae Chun, Seung Ryong Park
abstract: ArXiv:2610.41259v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) multiplexing has been limited in practice by the complexity and optical loss of the elements that separate the channels at the receiver side. Here we adopt the azimuthal harmonics of OAM petal patterns as the demultiplexing basis, which makes the receiver the optical counterpart of the circular antenna arrays used in radio OAM links: the petal pattern of topological charge [MATH] carries a single azimuthal harmonic of order [MATH], so one Fourier transform of the azimuthal intensity profile returns every channel, without gratings or mode sorters. The petals are formed by projecting a vector vortex beam from a single q-plate onto a linear polarization. A two-channel system at 515 nm with a 16-position circular photoreceiver array reaches 5.2 Gb/s below the forward error correction threshold, 2.6 Gb/s per channel from a 1.4 GHz photoreceiver.
tldr: The paper introduces an intensity-domain demultiplexing scheme for orbital angular momentum (OAM) channels that uses the azimuthal harmonics of OAM petal patterns, enabling single-Fourier-transform channel recovery in optical communication links.
motivation: OAM multiplexing for high-capacity optical links has been hampered by the complexity and insertion loss of receiver-side mode sorters and gratings, motivating a simpler demultiplexing architecture.
method: Petal patterns are generated by projecting a vector vortex beam from a single q-plate onto a linear polarization, and a circular photoreceiver array samples the azimuthal intensity profile so that one Fourier transform yields all channel harmonics.
result: A two-channel system at 515 nm with a 16-position circular photoreceiver array achieved 5.2 Gb/s below the FEC threshold, i.e. 2.6 Gb/s per channel with 1.4 GHz photoreceivers.
conclusion: Intensity-domain azimuthal-harmonic demultiplexing offers a grating-free, low-loss route to OAM multiplexing, analogous to circular antenna arrays in radio OAM links.

title: On The NP-Hardness Of Rank-Metric Minimum Distance And Syndrome Decoding, At Every Rate
authors: Venkata Gandikota, Vatsal Jha, S. Venkitesh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we investigate the hardness of computing minimum distance, as well as the hardness of syndrome decoding, for rank-metric codes. It is known (Gaborit and Z\'emor, IEEE TIT 2016) that for [MATH]-linear rank-metric codes of length [MATH], minimum distance when [MATH] and syndrome decoding when [MATH] are NP-hard under randomized reductions. We obtain a derandomization of these results and a bit more. We show that for any fixed small [MATH], for [MATH]-linear rank-metric codes of length [MATH] with [MATH], the problems of minimum distance, nearest codeword, and syndrome decoding are NP-hard under deterministic reductions. Further, we can prescribe the rate; that is, if we restrict to codes having any fixed rational rate [MATH], then the NP-hardness for all three problems persists. Our main technical contribution is simple, and possibly of independent interest. The reduction of Gaborit and Z\'emor (IEEE TIT 2016) relies on a distance-preserving embedding of a Hamming-metric code into a rank-metric code, obtained by multiplying its coordinates by a uniformly random vector. We show that we can choose an explicit vector from a slightly larger extension field.
tldr: The paper derandomizes and strengthens NP-hardness results for minimum distance, nearest codeword, and syndrome decoding of rank-metric codes, showing hardness persists at every fixed rational rate.
motivation: Prior NP-hardness results of Gaborit and Zémor for rank-metric codes relied on randomized reductions and only held in restricted parameter regimes; the authors aim to remove the randomness and to prescribe the code rate arbitrarily.
method: The reduction embeds a Hamming-metric code into a rank-metric code via coordinate-wise multiplication; the key technical step replaces the uniformly random multiplier vector with an explicit vector drawn from a slightly larger extension field, yielding deterministic reductions.
result: For any fixed small parameter and F_q-linear rank-metric codes of length n with the stated dimension constraints, minimum distance, nearest codeword, and syndrome decoding are NP-hard under deterministic reductions, and hardness holds at any fixed rational rate.
conclusion: The work gives a clean, simple derandomization of rank-metric code hardness results with rate-prescription, potentially of independent interest in coding theory and code-based cryptography.

title: A Basic Modal Logic For The Abstract Treatment Of Quantum Mixed States
authors: Tomoaki Kawano
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40803v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum logic has developed in various directions since its inception. However, many existing logical approaches either focus only on pure states, or use Hilbert-space models in which the abstract relationship between pure states, mixed states, and probabilities is not made explicit. In this work, we introduce a model designed to handle quantum mixed states abstractly. Furthermore, we construct a proof system for the proposed logic and establish its completeness with respect to the intended semantics.
tldr: The paper introduces a modal logic and complete proof system for an abstract treatment of quantum mixed states.
motivation: Existing quantum logics often focus only on pure states or rely on Hilbert-space models that do not explicitly capture the abstract relationships among pure states, mixed states, and probabilities.
method: The author defines a semantic model for quantum mixed states abstractly, constructs a proof system for the resulting logic, and proves completeness relative to the intended semantics.
result: A complete proof system is established for the proposed modal logic of abstract quantum mixed states.
conclusion: The work provides a foundational logical framework for reasoning about mixed states, but its contribution is primarily mathematical logic rather than quantum information theory or the other targeted research directions.

title: Quantum Manifestations Of Converse Symmetry Breaking
authors: Daniel P. Buser, Biswabibek Bandyopadhyay, Adilson E. Motter
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40762v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum synchronization holds promise in advancing quantum technologies such as sensing, communication, and computation. A key challenge in this rapidly developing field is to identify mechanisms that can promote the emergence of synchronous dynamics. Here, we show that quantum synchronization can be enhanced by introducing controlled heterogeneity in the form of coupling mismatches. Using spin van der Pol oscillators as a model system, we show that this mechanism constitutes a quantum analog of the phenomenon of converse symmetry breaking previously identified in classical oscillator networks, where a synchronous state is stabilized by explicit symmetry breaking. We quantify how quantum effects modify this behavior by tuning the degree of quantumness through variations of the spin quantum number. These findings suggest that quantum synchronization can be enhanced in experiments by harnessing rather than suppressing heterogeneity.
tldr: The paper shows that controlled coupling mismatches can enhance quantum synchronization in spin van der Pol oscillators, realizing a quantum analog of converse symmetry breaking.
motivation: Quantum synchronization could benefit quantum sensing, communication, and computation, but mechanisms to promote synchronous dynamics remain challenging to identify.
method: The authors study spin van der Pol oscillators and introduce heterogeneity via coupling mismatches, tuning the degree of quantumness through the spin quantum number.
result: They find that explicit symmetry breaking through coupling mismatches stabilizes synchronous states, and quantum effects modify this behavior depending on the spin quantum number.
conclusion: The work suggests that experiments can enhance quantum synchronization by harnessing rather than suppressing heterogeneity, extending converse symmetry breaking to the quantum regime.

title: Benchmarking One-Dimensional Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Methods On Quantum Hardware
authors: Lucy T. Zhang Melvina Quartey (rensselaer Polytechnic Institute)
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical computational fluid dynamics (CFD) methods encounter significant computational bottlenecks in large systems and at high Reynolds number flows due to the rapid increase in degrees of freedom, even on flagship supercomputers. As quantum computers emerge, the Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Method (QLBM) has been proposed as a quantum-native alternative for solving fluid dynamics problems. However, until recently, nearly all studies have relied on classical quantum simulators rather than real quantum hardware. This study presents a benchmark of a one-dimensional QLBM implementation executed on three different IBM Quantum hardware. We design and test a quantum circuit for the advection-diffusion equation using amplitude encoding, a Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK)-type collision operator, and a streaming step with periodic boundary conditions. Our numerical experiments evaluate transpiled two-qubit gate count, total circuit depth, runtime, and accuracy metrics including maximum absolute error ([MATH] norm) and root-mean-square error (RMSE). We find that the present collision and streaming operators dominate the overall cost and become the primary scalability bottleneck on current hardware. To mitigate the prohibitive cost of full quantum state tomography on hardware-based benchmarking exercises, we introduce a sampler-based measurement strategy that reconstructs macroscopic density fields directly from computational-basis measurements. This approach substantially reduces measurement overhead while preserving the expected advection-diffusion dynamics on hardware. These results provide a quantitative assessment of QLBM performance in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) regime and identify the principal algorithmic and experimental limitations that must be addressed for QLBM to become viable for fluid dynamics.
tldr: A benchmark of a one-dimensional quantum lattice Boltzmann method for advection-diffusion, executed on three IBM quantum processors.
motivation: Classical CFD becomes intractable at high Reynolds numbers and large system sizes, motivating quantum-native solvers, yet almost all QLBM studies so far have used simulators rather than real hardware.
method: The authors design a circuit using amplitude encoding, a BGK-type collision operator, and a periodic-boundary streaming step, then transpile and run it on IBM hardware, evaluating two-qubit gate counts, depth, runtime, and error metrics, plus a sampler-based measurement scheme that reconstructs density fields from computational-basis samples instead of full tomography.
result: Collision and streaming operators dominate circuit cost and form the principal scalability bottleneck on NISQ devices; the sampler-based measurement strategy substantially reduces measurement overhead while preserving the expected advection-diffusion dynamics.
conclusion: QLBM is currently limited by operator cost and hardware noise; the paper quantifies these limitations and identifies algorithmic and experimental obstacles to making QLBM viable for fluid dynamics.

title: Scaling Limits As Extensions Of Continuous Bundles Of C*-algebras
authors: Benjamin H. Feintzeig Kade Cicchella
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze scaling limits in algebraic quantum field theory using continuous bundles of C*-algebras. Different conditions of continuity on such bundles encode different strengths of approximation of the theory by its scaling limit. As a proof of concept, we consider the small-distance scaling limit of the theory of a massive free scalar field, which corresponds to a massless free scalar field. We provide a number of examples of local algebras of observables for which the corresponding bundle of C*-algebras representing the scaling limit is merely lower semicontinuous. Further, we construct an algebra of nonlocal observables for which the corresponding bundle of C*-algebras representing the scaling limit is uniformly continuous.
tldr: The paper analyzes scaling limits in algebraic quantum field theory using continuous bundles of C*-algebras, with the massive free scalar field as a proof-of-concept.
motivation: Scaling limits are central to relating quantum field theories at different energy or distance scales, and the authors aim to formalize different strengths of approximation via continuity conditions on C*-algebra bundles.
method: They employ continuous bundles of C*-algebras and study lower semicontinuity versus uniform continuity for local algebras of observables, applying the framework to the small-distance limit from a massive to a massless free scalar field.
result: They provide examples of local observable algebras whose scaling-limit bundles are merely lower semicontinuous, and construct a nonlocal observable algebra yielding a uniformly continuous bundle.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that continuous-bundle techniques can distinguish strengths of scaling-limit approximations in AQFT, extending the framework beyond standard local algebras.

title: Quantum Vehicle Routing Problem: A Smart Initialization Strategy For Ill-conditioned Optimization Landscapes
authors: Emanuele Casciaro, Mario de Simone, Stefano Martina, Fabio Mascherpa, Alfonso Amendola, Filippo Caruso
abstract: ArXiv:2610.41120v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the expansion of complex transport infrastructure, new paths for linking different destinations have emerged, allowing the definition of multiple routes. The introduction of new roads may also lead to disruptions in traffic flow. This problem can be generalized into a special case of VRP, which aims to find the optimal route for a fleet of vehicles within a network of destinations. Finding solutions to this problem requires an exponential number of operations, hindering the ability of exact solvers to deal with large instances, which must therefore be tackled using heuristics, often leading to suboptimal results. Quantum-based algorithms may allow us to find exact solutions in polynomial time with high probability, offering a potential future alternative to classical solvers and in this work, we focus on the QAOA. Our novel contributions are a parameter-initialization strategy that improves the convergence probability and the integration of the subtour constraints directly into the optimization without using additional qubits by employing an approximation of exponential equality constraints. We believe that our results pave the way for effectively solving instances of VRP using quantum-based solutions, leveraging the space-efficient problem encoding and our initialization strategy, which limits the effect of barren-plateau under random parameter initialization.
tldr: The paper proposes a QAOA-based approach for the vehicle routing problem with a novel parameter-initialization strategy and space-efficient subtour constraints.
motivation: Vehicle routing problems are computationally hard for exact classical solvers at large scale, motivating quantum approximate optimization approaches that may find high-quality solutions efficiently.
method: The authors use the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) with a tailored parameter-initialization scheme and integrate subtour constraints directly into the optimization via an approximation of exponential equality constraints without extra qubits.
result: The proposed initialization strategy improves convergence probability and helps mitigate barren plateaus under random parameter initialization, while the constraint encoding reduces qubit overhead.
conclusion: The work suggests that space-efficient QAOA encodings and smart initialization can enable more effective quantum solutions to vehicle routing instances, though it remains an application-focused optimization study.

title: Parametric Enhancement Of An Optical Spring In A Dark Signal-Recycling Cavity
authors: Kaido Suzuki, Ryo Iden, Ken-Ichi Harada, Kentaro Somiya
abstract: ArXiv:2610.41270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical springs tailor the response of precision sensors. Parametric amplification of the signal field stiffens the spring, extending the precision to higher frequencies. A Michelson interferometer operated at a dark fringe is the most direct way to separate the signal from the carrier for amplification. We experimentally demonstrate such quantum manipulation of the optical spring by placing an optical parametric amplifier in a cavity at the dark port, showing a significant increase of the optical-spring constant with the parametric gain within a factor of four below the oscillation threshold.
tldr: The paper experimentally enhances an optical spring in a dark-fringe Michelson interferometer by placing an optical parametric amplifier in a dark-port cavity.
motivation: Optical springs can tailor precision-sensor response, and parametric amplification of the signal field may extend sensitivity to higher frequencies.
method: They operate a Michelson interferometer at dark fringe to separate signal from carrier and insert an optical parametric amplifier in a cavity at the dark port, measuring the optical-spring constant versus parametric gain.
result: The optical-spring constant increases significantly with parametric gain while remaining below the oscillation threshold by up to a factor of four.
conclusion: This demonstrates quantum manipulation of optical springs for improved high-frequency precision sensing.

title: Quantifying Blinking Suppression And Probing Its Mechanism In PPD-Treated Single Quantum Dots
authors: Eduard A. Podshivaylov, Egor B. Kurgin, Changgang Yang, Guofeng Zhang, Pavel A. Frantsuzov
abstract: ArXiv:2610.41285v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Colloidal semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) are highly promising materials for various applications, yet photoluminescence intermittency (blinking) remains a key obstacle to their practical use. While recent advances have enabled partial or complete suppression of this effect, both the degree of suppression and the mechanism by which it occurs are often difficult to establish. In the present work we analyse the blinking suppression of single CdSe/ZnS QDs after treatment with p-phenylenediamine (PPD), recently discovered by Yang et al. We revisit the blinking mechanism in this system and show that it is governed predominantly by the trapping mechanism, rather than by Auger ionization as previously proposed. For data analysis we apply a threshold-free two-dimensional criterion recently proposed by Podshivaylov and Frantsuzov. The criterion is based on the relative quantum yield estimator [MATH] and the decay-rate fluctuation parameter [MATH]. We found that PPD treatment significantly increases the relative quantum yield and leads to only a modest increase in [MATH], indicating that the dominant effect of PPD is to shift the distribution of the non-radiative recombination rate toward lower values, rather than to eliminate its fluctuations. We further suggest a number of possible mechanisms of PPD-induced suppression and propose critical experiments for their verification.
tldr: A statistical analysis of photoluminescence blinking suppression in PPD-treated single CdSe/ZnS colloidal quantum dots, arguing the suppression arises from a trapping mechanism rather than Auger ionization.
motivation: Blinking (photoluminescence intermittency) in colloidal quantum dots hinders their practical use, and while chemical treatments such as p-phenylenediamine (PPD) can partially or fully suppress it, both the degree of suppression and the underlying mechanism remain poorly characterized.
method: The authors reanalyze single-dot blinking trajectories after PPD treatment using a threshold-free two-dimensional criterion based on a relative quantum yield estimator and a decay-rate fluctuation parameter, and compare competing blinking models (trapping vs. Auger ionization).
result: PPD treatment substantially increases the relative quantum yield while only modestly increasing the decay-rate fluctuation parameter, indicating that PPD shifts the non-radiative recombination rate distribution toward lower values rather than eliminating its fluctuations; the data favor the trapping mechanism over Auger ionization.
conclusion: The dominant effect of PPD is suppression of non-radiative rates rather than removal of their fluctuations, and the authors propose candidate microscopic mechanisms plus critical experiments to discriminate among them.

title: Fgsm Attack Transferability From Simulation To Quantum Hardware In Network Intrusion Detection
authors: Zeeshan Ajmal, Kimmo Halunen, Marc Mau{\ss}ner, Volker Reers, Arif Ali Khan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40701v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computers are now available through cloud platforms, and recent work has proposed using them to detect network intrusions. It is not yet clear how easily such systems can be attacked. We train a hybrid variational quantum classifier (VQC) on the Friday DDoS subset of CICIDS2017 and test it against two attacks: label flipping during training and FGSM evasion at prediction time. We run the tests in simulation and on IBM hardware, the Fez superconducting processor (Heron r2). We find that two models with similar accuracy can differ greatly in how easily they are attacked. A model that decides with little confidence loses half its detections to a very small change in the input, while a model trained to decide with more confidence needs a much larger change before it fails. Attacks built in simulation against the more confident model also work on real hardware, and the device classifies every unaltered attack sample correctly. Simulated device noise does not reduce accuracy, but it does reduce the model's confidence and makes attacks easier, so accuracy alone does not show how exposed a model is. Label flipping has no measurable effect until 15% of attack labels are changed. These results show that device noise should not be treated as a defense and that reported weaknesses in these classifiers depend partly on how they were trained.
tldr: The paper studies adversarial robustness of a hybrid variational quantum classifier for network intrusion detection, comparing simulation with execution on an IBM Heron r2 superconducting processor.
motivation: Cloud-accessible quantum computers have been proposed for network intrusion detection, but it is unclear how easily such classifiers can be attacked via training-time label flipping or prediction-time FGSM evasion.
method: A variational quantum classifier is trained on the Friday DDoS subset of CICIDS2017 and evaluated against label-flipping poisoning and FGSM evasion attacks, both in noiseless/noisy simulation and on real IBM hardware.
result: Models with similar accuracy differ strongly in vulnerability: low-confidence models lose about half their detections under tiny input perturbations, while high-confidence models require much larger perturbations; simulated device noise lowers confidence and eases attacks without reducing accuracy, and label flipping matters only beyond 15% corruption.
conclusion: Device noise should not be treated as a defense, and reported vulnerabilities of quantum classifiers depend substantially on training choices; accuracy alone is an inadequate measure of exposure.

title: On The Reconstruction Of Orthomodular Logic Via Restricted Negation
authors: Ryo Kashima Tomoaki Kawano (kanagawa University)
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40807v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Orthomodular logic has long been studied as a fundamental logical framework within quantum logic. In addition to its lattice-theoretic foundations, various formulations have been proposed that incorporate specialized implication connectives and more complex logical connectives. In this study, we reconstruct orthomodular logic by introducing a connective referred to as restricted negation, which has received comparatively little attention in the existing literature. We demonstrate that this connective provides a natural and expressive basis for formulating the core principles of orthomodular logic. Furthermore, as a main result, we construct a new proof system for orthomodular logic founded on this connective.
tldr: The paper reconstructs orthomodular logic using a restricted negation connective and introduces a new proof system for it.
motivation: Orthomodular logic is a foundational framework in quantum logic, and the authors aim to provide a more natural and expressive formulation using a neglected connective.
method: They introduce restricted negation as a basis for expressing core principles of orthomodular logic and construct a proof system founded on this connective.
result: The main result is a new proof system for orthomodular logic based on restricted negation, argued to naturally capture its core principles.
conclusion: The work offers a logical reconstruction of orthomodular logic, but it is foundational quantum logic rather than quantum information theory or the other specified research directions.

title: Finite-Element Electromagnetic Analysis And Evaluation Of Antenna Performance Metrics Using A Quantum Linear System Solver
authors: Hiroaki Ominato, Takahiro Ohyama, Shiro Kawabata
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electromagnetic analysis based on the finite element method is widely used in antenna design. At higher frequencies, however, the required mesh refinement makes solving large sparse linear systems the main contributor to computational cost. Quantum linear system solvers offer a potential means of accelerating this step, but their output is a superposition state: reconstructing all components of the classical solution vector would forfeit the quantum speedup. Prior studies have proposed methods for obtaining physical quantities such as scattering cross sections and scattering parameters from the solution state. To support antenna design using fault-tolerant quantum computers, we formulate the total radiated power, the radiated power within a prescribed solid angle, and the dielectric and conductive losses as observables for efficient evaluation from a quantum solution state. These observables avoid the measurement cost of reconstructing all components of the output quantum state. We develop an end-to-end hybrid quantum--classical workflow that combines finite-element electromagnetic analysis, matrix preconditioning, a quantum linear system solver, and the evaluation of antenna design metrics. To validate the workflow, we performed numerical experiments evaluating these observables for an axisymmetric coaxially fed monopole antenna. Under idealized conditions, the relative errors in the total radiated power and the dissipated power with respect to the classical finite-element solution were on the order of [MATH], confirming the consistency of the workflow. The proposed method is expected to provide a basis for using quantum linear system solvers to evaluate antenna performance and, in the future, to design high-frequency wireless devices.
tldr: The authors formulate antenna performance metrics (total radiated power, power radiated into a solid angle, dielectric and conductive losses) as observables that can be extracted from the output state of a quantum linear system solver, and demonstrate an end-to-end hybrid quantum-classical finite-element workflow on a coaxially fed monopole antenna.
motivation: Finite-element electromagnetic analysis for high-frequency antenna design is dominated by the cost of solving large sparse linear systems, and quantum linear system solvers could accelerate this step—but reading out the full classical solution vector would destroy the quantum speedup.
method: The paper casts the finite-element Maxwell problem into a linear system, applies matrix preconditioning, solves it with a fault-tolerant quantum linear system algorithm, and computes antenna metrics as expectation values of carefully designed observables rather than reconstructing the full solution; numerical experiments are performed for an axisymmetric monopole antenna.
result: Under idealized conditions, relative errors in total radiated power and dissipated power with respect to the classical finite-element solution were on the order of the stated tolerance, confirming consistency of the hybrid workflow.
conclusion: The work provides a basis for using quantum linear system solvers in antenna performance evaluation and, prospectively, in designing high-frequency wireless devices, though practical quantum advantage remains contingent on fault-tolerant hardware.

title: Hypergraph Cycle Enumeration For Efficient Inference Of Planted k-XOR With Smooth Trade-off
authors: Arman Babakhani, Enrico Fontana, Junhyung Lyle Kim, Shouvanik Chakrabarti, Ruslan Shaydulin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce hypergraph cycle enumeration (HCE), a simple spectral framework for detecting and recovering planted signals in noisy hypergraph inference problems. We study HCE on one representative problem from this class, namely planted noisy k-XOR, also known as sparse Learning Parity with Noise (LPN). Both theoretically and empirically, HCE achieves comparable recovery behavior to Kikuchi method, matching Kikuchi hierarchy. We identify parameter regimes where HCE outperforms Kikuchi method, showing that neither algorithm is universally better. We also show a subquadratic quantum speedup for HCE by replacing one of the algorithm's steps with a quantum walk. Our classical and quantum algorithms do not refute the quartic quantum speedup of quantum Kikuchi method, which remains valid for the practically relevant regime of large size and high noise strength.
tldr: The paper introduces hypergraph cycle enumeration (HCE), a spectral method for planted noisy k-XOR/sparse LPN inference, with a subquadratic quantum speedup via quantum walk.
motivation: The authors aim to develop a simple spectral framework for detecting and recovering planted signals in noisy hypergraph inference problems, focusing on planted noisy k-XOR as a representative case.
method: HCE uses hypergraph cycle enumeration as a spectral algorithm and replaces one step with a quantum walk to obtain a subquadratic quantum speedup; performance is compared theoretically and empirically with the Kikuchi method.
result: HCE achieves recovery behavior comparable to the Kikuchi method and matches the Kikuchi hierarchy in some regimes, while outperforming it in others; the quantum version gives a subquadratic speedup but does not refute the quartic quantum speedup of quantum Kikuchi.
conclusion: Neither HCE nor Kikuchi is universally better, and the quartic quantum speedup of quantum Kikuchi remains valid for large-size, high-noise regimes.

title: Which Adiabatic Cycles Alter An Action Variable?
authors: Taksu Cheon Atushi Tanaka
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40671v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Action variables are adiabatic invariants: their values are preserved during adiabatic time evolutions in completely integrable classical Hamiltonian systems. Nevertheless, an adiabatic cycle can alter how an action variable depends on phase-space variables that are independent of adiabatic parameters. Such a change, which we call action variable holonomy, induces adiabatic torus pumping in phase space. For a family of completely integrable kicked-top systems, a homotopy classification of adiabatic cycles identifies which adiabatic cycles induce action variable holonomy and adiabatic torus pumping. A physical example is also provided.
tldr: This paper classifies adiabatic cycles in completely integrable kicked-top systems that induce holonomy of action variables and adiabatic torus pumping.
motivation: Action variables are usually adiabatic invariants, but certain adiabatic cycles can change their dependence on phase-space variables, a phenomenon the authors call action-variable holonomy.
method: The authors use a homotopy classification of adiabatic cycles for a family of completely integrable kicked-top systems and provide a physical example.
result: The classification identifies which adiabatic cycles produce action-variable holonomy and thereby induce adiabatic torus pumping in phase space.
conclusion: Adiabatic cycles in integrable classical Hamiltonian systems can alter action-variable dependence and generate geometric pumping effects.

title: Predictive Maintenance At The Edge: An Embedded Anomaly Detection Pipeline Trained With Quantum Optimization
authors: Filipe Chagas Ferraz
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40848v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article presents a predictive-maintenance pipeline that detects anomalies in bearings from vibration signals, adapted for deployment at the edge on low-cost microcontrollers, and that uses quantum optimization in two steps of its training. The pipeline consists of a step of vibration feature extraction and a step of classification with a one-class support vector machine (OCSVM). The features are selected by minimum redundancy and maximum relevance (mRMR) with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), under a limit on computing time. The OCSVM is adapted for inference at the edge without floating-point operations and is trained by a variational quantum algorithm with Pauli-correlation encoding (PCE). In small-scale tests on a simulator, with the Paderborn bearing dataset, the VQE found the optimal selection in 36% of the runs with Adam, and PCE chose better support vectors than chance, until a classical local search made the two equal. A classical baseline, the usual OCSVM trained by SMO with its weights rounded, matched them without any search.
tldr: An edge-deployable bearing-fault anomaly-detection pipeline in which feature selection (mRMR) and one-class SVM training are partially driven by variational quantum algorithms (VQE and Pauli-correlation encoding).
motivation: The author aims to bring predictive maintenance to low-cost microcontrollers while exploring whether near-term quantum optimization can improve classical machine-learning training steps under tight compute budgets.
method: Vibration features are extracted and selected via mRMR with a VQE under a time limit; a fixed-point-free one-class SVM is trained using a variational quantum algorithm with Pauli-correlation encoding, then benchmarked on the Paderborn bearing dataset using a simulator.
result: VQE with Adam found the optimal feature selection in 36% of runs, and PCE selected better support vectors than chance, but a classical local search matched it, and a standard SMO-trained OCSVM with rounded weights matched both without any search.
conclusion: The quantum-assisted training offers no clear advantage over simple classical baselines in these small-scale simulations, so the practical value lies mainly in the embedded, floating-point-free edge implementation.

title: Faster-than-power-law Decay Of Order Parameter Correlations In The Two-dimensional Rp$^2$ Model: A Rigorous Result By Vibe-proving
authors: Masaki Oshikawa
abstract: ArXiv:2610.41256v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the RP[MATH] model on the two-dimensional square lattice with nearest-neighbor interactions. It is obtained by replacing the spin in the standard classical Heisenberg model with a director, which does not distinguish two opposite directions. Unlike the standard classical Heisenberg model or the O(3) nonlinear sigma model, the RP[MATH] (and its cousin RP[MATH]) model allows point vortex defects classified by [MATH] in two dimensions. It is tempting to expect the [MATH] vortices to induce a phase transition analogous to the well-established Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in the O(2) model (XY model) in two dimensions. Indeed, the possibilities of a critical phase or a critical point with power-law correlations of the order parameter in the RP[MATH] and RP[MATH] models have been discussed in the literature. However, the challenging nature of the problem has prevented a definitive conclusion on the phase diagram so far. In this paper, we report a rigorous mathematical proof by Artificial Intelligence (ChatGPT 6 Astra) that the absolute value of the two-point correlation function of order parameters at distance [MATH] in the RP[MATH] and RP[MATH] models on the two-dimensional square lattice is bounded above by [MATH] for any finite inverse temperature [MATH], with positive constants [MATH] and [MATH] depending only on [MATH]. Namely, the correlation function decays faster than any power of [MATH]. The proof is formalized and verified in Lean; the formalization is publicly available at doi:10.5281/zenodo.23548847 . A heuristic argument based on a one-parameter effective theory ansatz at large distances combined with the rigorous correlation bound suggests (but does not prove) that the [MATH] vortices are always unbound at any nonzero temperature.
tldr: A rigorous (Lean-formalized, AI-assisted) proof that order-parameter correlations in the two-dimensional RP^2 and RP^3 director models decay faster than any power law at all finite temperatures, with a heuristic argument that Z_2 vortices remain unbound at any nonzero temperature.
motivation: The RP^2 model, unlike the Heisenberg or O(3) sigma model, admits point vortex defects classified by Z_2 in two dimensions, raising the question of whether they support a BKT-like critical phase with power-law order-parameter correlations; the issue had remained unresolved.
method: An analytic proof (reported as generated by an AI system and verified in the Lean proof assistant) bounding the two-point order-parameter correlation function by exp(-c (ln r)^2 / beta)-type decay, combined with a one-parameter effective field theory ansatz at large distances.
result: The absolute value of the two-point correlation function at distance r is bounded above by a super-polynomially decaying function for any finite inverse temperature beta, so correlations decay faster than any power of r.
conclusion: The RP^2/RP^3 models on the square lattice lack the power-law critical phase one might have expected; the heuristic effective-theory argument further suggests Z_2 vortices are unbound at all nonzero temperatures, though this is not proven.

title: Non-contact Temperature Sensing And Optical Scatter In Cryogenically-cooled Crystalline Silicon
authors: Disha Pankaj Kapasi, Travis Counihan, Kevin Kimes, Alina Sendowsky, Alexandra Gruson, Daniel Martinez, Michael Rezac, Kevin Silverio, Sean Sorto, Joshua R. Smith
abstract: ArXiv:2610.41261v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cryogenic crystalline silicon is a promising optical material for next generation gravitational-wave detectors due to its low mechanical loss (a driver of thermal noise), high thermal conductivity and zero coefficient of thermal expansion at 123 K. In this paper, we report on the design and results of an experiment to measure the temperature of a flat-flat uncoated crystalline silicon sample using a non-contact sensing method relying on interference (optical fringes) made from reflections between the front and back surfaces. We also propose a scheme for implementation of this technique for cryogenic test masses in future gravitational-wave detectors such as Einstein Telescope and LIGO Voyager. Additionally, we characterize the optical scattering of the sample in vacuum at cryogenic temperatures by using a high-sensitivity infrared camera. We measured relatively constant scatter with an average bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) of [MATH] at a scattering angle of [MATH] over the (cold-plate) temperature range of 123-294 K and saw no evidence for growth of cryogenic molecular layers (ice) on the sample in our current setup.
tldr: The paper demonstrates non-contact temperature sensing and characterizes optical scattering of cryogenically cooled crystalline silicon for future gravitational-wave detector test masses.
motivation: Cryogenic crystalline silicon is attractive for next-generation gravitational-wave detectors due to low mechanical loss and favorable thermal properties, but practical temperature monitoring and optical scattering at cryogenic temperatures need characterization.
method: The authors use optical interference fringes from front- and back-surface reflections to infer the temperature of an uncoated flat silicon sample, and they measure optical scatter in vacuum from 123–294 K using a high-sensitivity infrared camera.
result: They observe relatively constant scatter with an average BRDF over the cold-plate temperature range and find no evidence of cryogenic molecular layer growth in their setup; they also propose implementing the sensing technique for future detector test masses.
conclusion: The work supports the development of cryogenic silicon optics for gravitational-wave detectors but is not directly connected to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: ZenKO: Guided And Iterative Quantum-Classical Method For Molecular Electronic Structure Using Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization
authors: Devesh Tiwari Aditya Ranjan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.41146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The electronic structure of molecules is foundational for scientific advancement, however determining it remains challenging due to the growth of the molecular Hilbert space with system size. Recent approaches address this by using quantum circuits to sample candidate configurations and sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) to compute the ground state. We propose ZenKO, a novel gradient-based, iterative SQD method that employs a hybrid quantum-classical approach. ZenKO decomposes configuration selection into discovery, validation, and refinement, enabling targeted subspace expansion and guided exploration. Our evaluation demonstrates that, across [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] molecules, ZenKO improves ground-state accuracy compared to prior iterative methods, while significantly reducing classical cost.
tldr: ZenKO is a hybrid quantum-classical iterative method for molecular electronic structure that uses gradient-guided sample-based quantum diagonalization to select and refine configuration subspaces.
motivation: Molecular electronic structure calculations are limited by Hilbert-space growth, motivating quantum sampling combined with classical diagonalization to approximate ground states.
method: The authors propose ZenKO, a gradient-based iterative SQD approach that decomposes configuration selection into discovery, validation, and refinement stages for targeted subspace expansion.
result: Across several molecules, ZenKO improves ground-state accuracy over prior iterative SQD methods while significantly reducing classical computational cost.
conclusion: ZenKO offers a guided and efficient quantum-classical workflow for molecular ground-state estimation, but it is primarily a quantum chemistry algorithm rather than a contribution to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Existence And Stability Of Weyl Points
authors: Michael I. Weinstein Curtiss Lyman
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40963v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weyl points are quasimomentum-energy pairs in the band structure of three-dimensional periodic media at which two dispersion surfaces touch conically. They first arose in a model introduced by H. Weyl in 1929, but were first observed only recently in condensed matter physics and photonics experiments. Weyl points have been explored theoretically via numerical computation and via tight binding (discrete) models. In this article we present the first analytical treatment of Weyl points in a continuum PDE-type model. Starting with a Schr\"odinger operator whose electric potential is periodic with respect to the body-centered cubic (BCC) lattice, we introduce a small BCC-periodic magnetic vector potential that is equivariant with respect to a specific abelian group of symmetries. For magnetic Schr\"odinger operators of this type, we prove (i) that a pair of Weyl points bifurcates from a threefold degeneracy in the band structure of the underlying non-magnetic operator, and (ii) that these Weyl points are stable against small self-adjoint BCC-periodic perturbations of both the electric and magnetic vector potentials.
tldr: An analytical proof that Weyl points bifurcate from a threefold band degeneracy in a continuum magnetic Schrödinger operator with BCC-periodic potentials, and that they are stable under small periodic perturbations.
motivation: Weyl points have so far been studied numerically or in discrete tight-binding models; the authors aim to provide the first rigorous analytical treatment in a continuum PDE setting.
method: Spectral analysis of a Schrödinger operator with BCC-periodic electric potential perturbed by a small symmetry-equivariant BCC-periodic magnetic vector potential, using bifurcation theory and perturbation arguments for self-adjoint operators.
result: A pair of Weyl points is shown to bifurcate from a threefold degeneracy of the non-magnetic operator, and these points persist (are stable) under small self-adjoint BCC-periodic perturbations of both electric and magnetic potentials.
conclusion: Establishes rigorous existence and stability of Weyl points in continuum periodic media, providing a mathematically solid foundation for the physics of conical band crossings.

title: Machine Learning-Enabled Time-Skipping Method: Theory And Perturbation-Based Verification
authors: Isaac C. Bannerman, Shaowu Pan, Lucy T. Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.41152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulating the time evolution of practical mechanics problems requires many time steps. This cost is further compounded by the iterative nature of implicit solvers. We present a cycle-based Machine Learning-enabled Time-skipping (MLT) method. In each cycle, several time steps are skipped, a machine learning (ML) prediction bridges the gap to initialize one solver step, and the physics-based solver then runs for several steps to correct any accumulated errors. Using the Implicit Function Theorem, we derive first-order estimates that characterize how ML prediction errors propagate. These estimates identify when errors remain bounded across cycles and guide the choice of cycle parameters, independent of model architecture. We verify these estimates on the Allen-Cahn equation and a forced variant using controlled synthetic perturbations that emulate ML errors. Wall-clock measurements confirm the theoretical speedup is realizable in practice. The MLT method provides a robust framework for accelerating time-marching in dynamic simulations.
tldr: The paper introduces a machine-learning-enabled time-skipping method to accelerate numerical time-marching simulations of mechanics problems.
motivation: Simulating practical mechanics problems requires many time steps, especially with implicit solvers, making conventional time integration computationally expensive.
method: The MLT method skips several time steps per cycle, uses ML prediction to initialize a solver step, then runs the physics solver for correction; first-order error propagation estimates are derived via the Implicit Function Theorem.
result: Theoretical error estimates are verified on the Allen-Cahn equation and a forced variant using synthetic perturbations, and wall-clock measurements confirm practical speedup.
conclusion: MLT provides a robust framework for accelerating time-marching in dynamic simulations, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Coordination Three Heals, Coordination Four Is Hard: The Antiferromagnetic Potts Model With A Costly Third State
authors: Jeehoon Choi, Suhwan Yoo, Chaeyeon Kim, Hee Young Kwon, Changyeon Won
abstract: ArXiv:2610.41277v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the ground states of the antiferromagnetic three-state Potts model in which the third state carries a single-ion energy cost [MATH], on arbitrary lattices, and show that the difficulty of the ground-state problem is controlled by the maximum coordination [MATH] alone; on planar lattices with [MATH] it is classified completely. On lattices with coordination at most three the third state heals frustrated bonds one for one: every graph of maximum degree three other than [MATH] has an independent set of sites that meets every odd cycle and whose size equals the number [MATH] of frustrated bonds of the Ising ground state. This identity also follows from known results on the chromatic vertex stability of graphs; we give a constructive proof. Hence [MATH] for all [MATH], computable in polynomial time on planar lattices. In graph-theoretic terms, independent odd cycle transversal is solvable in polynomial time on planar subcubic graphs. On planar lattices with maximum coordination four, in contrast, deciding the ground-state energy is NP-complete for every fixed [MATH] and polynomial for [MATH]. The boundary is set by a local principle: a site of coordination [MATH] in the third state relieves at most [MATH] frustrated bonds, so the third state is useless once [MATH]; this threshold is sharp for every [MATH] and reproduces the triangular-lattice point [MATH] of the equivalent spin-1 Blume--Capel antiferromagnet. From a single Ising ground state the proof builds an exact ground state in polynomial time, which for quasicrystalline, foam-like and defective lattices with thousands of sites takes seconds to minutes.
tldr: The ground-state problem of the antiferromagnetic three-state Potts model with a costly third state is shown to be governed entirely by the lattice's maximum coordination number, being polynomially solvable for coordination ≤3 and NP-complete for planar coordination-4 lattices.
motivation: Frustrated antiferromagnetic Potts and Blume-Capel models are classically hard, and the authors want to pin down exactly which structural lattice parameter controls the computational complexity of finding ground states.
method: Graph-theoretic analysis relating independent odd-cycle transversals to frustrated-bond counts, with a constructive polynomial-time algorithm for subcubic graphs and NP-completeness reductions for planar maximum-degree-four lattices.
result: For maximum degree three, an independent set meeting every odd cycle has size equal to the number of frustrated bonds of the Ising ground state, giving a polynomial-time computable energy; for planar coordination four the decision problem is NP-complete for every fixed cost, with a sharp local threshold.
conclusion: Coordination number alone determines the tractability of these Potts ground states, yielding fast exact ground states for quasicrystalline, foam-like, and defective lattices with thousands of sites.

title: The Maximal Determinant Of Order 15 Over The Third Roots Of Unity
authors: Daoyu Dong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40679v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the largest absolute determinant of a [MATH] matrix with entries in [MATH], where [MATH] and [MATH], is [MATH]. A matrix attaining this value was already known; the issue is maximality. The proof follows the Gram-matrix search method used in the real maximal-determinant problem. A sharp determinant bound in terms of the off-diagonal Gram energy, combined with Eisenstein congruences and a published classification of difference matrices, reduces a strict improvement to 23 possible energies. Componentwise Schur bounds and exact support catalogues then leave a small number of cases, excluded by orthogonality, rank, and spectral-intertwining conditions. We present the finite tests in a common framework and supply their replay programs. For the displayed extremizer we give a dephased representative, its Gram matrix and spectrum, and an exact computation of its monomial automorphism group, which has order 1008. The proof determines the value of the maximum, but does not classify all equality cases.
tldr: The paper proves that the maximal absolute determinant of a 15x15 matrix with entries in the third roots of unity is attained by a known matrix, closing the maximality question via a Gram-matrix search.
motivation: The maximal determinant problem over roots of unity generalizes the classical real (and complex) maximal determinant problem; for order 15 over Eisenstein integers only a candidate extremizer was known, but not its optimality.
method: A sharp determinant bound in terms of off-diagonal Gram energy, combined with Eisenstein congruences and a published classification of difference matrices, reduces any strict improvement to 23 candidate energies; componentwise Schur bounds and exact support catalogues then reduce to finitely many cases excluded by orthogonality, rank, and spectral-intertwining arguments, with replay programs supplied.
result: The maximum determinant value is proven, and the extremizer is characterized by a dephased representative, its Gram matrix and spectrum, and an exact monomial automorphism group of order 1008.
conclusion: The maximum is determined although equality cases are not fully classified; the framework is a reusable computational-algebraic approach to maximal determinant problems over algebraic integer rings.

title: Bernstein And Stieltjes Properties Of Some Functions Involving Logarithmic Functions
authors: Feng Qi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40718v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that [MATH], with [MATH], is a complete Bernstein function and give its L\'evy measure explicitly. For [MATH], we prove that [MATH] is not a Stieltjes function, so [MATH] is not a complete Bernstein function, but [MATH] is a Bernstein function. The latter rests on the positivity of a function built from the convolution of the exponential integrals [MATH] and [MATH]. We also give a related completely monotonic function that is not a Stieltjes function.
tldr: A pure mathematical analysis establishing complete Bernstein, Stieltjes, and Bernstein properties for certain functions built from logarithmic and exponential-integral terms.
motivation: The author aims to classify specific elementary functions (involving logarithms and exponential integrals) within the theory of Bernstein and Stieltjes functions, determining complete monotonicity through convolution positivity.
method: Explicit construction of the Lévy measure for one function to prove it is a complete Bernstein function, plus a proof via positivity of a convolution of exponential integrals that another function fails the Stieltjes property yet remains a Bernstein function.
result: One function with parameter constraints is shown to be a complete Bernstein function with explicitly given Lévy measure; for another parameter regime the function is shown not to be Stieltjes (hence not complete Bernstein) but still Bernstein; a related completely monotonic non-Stieltjes function is also identified.
conclusion: The work sharpens the classification of analytic functions arising from logarithmic and exponential-integral expressions, contributing results to classical function theory rather than to any quantum-information or thermodynamic application.

title: Box-Cone Representations Of Bound-Factor Rlt Constraints In Semidefinite Relaxations
authors: Katherine Charbonneau, Hao Hu, Renata Sotirov
abstract: ArXiv:2610.41051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear inequalities can generate large constraint systems in semidefinite relaxations of binary quadratic programs, making the quadratic subproblems of splitting methods expensive to solve. We develop a box-cone representation of bound-factor reformulation-linearization technique (RLT) constraints in semidefinite relaxations of binary quadratic programs. These constraints arise by multiplying each original linear inequality by every binary variable and its complement and linearizing the resulting products. Our key observation is that all products generated by one inequality share a common slack and admit an exact representation in the standard cone over the unit box. This box-cone representation processes the inequalities through independent explicit projections, without introducing a separate nonnegative slack for each scalar RLT inequality. We illustrate the computational use of the representation within standard two-block alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). The resulting subproblems require linear solves with a reusable factorization and explicit cone projections, without enlarging the semidefinite matrix. Experiments on 257 binary quadratic programs compare this implementation with SDPNAL+. A second application groups Max-Cut triangle inequalities into box cones and uses the resulting bounds within an existing branch-and-bound framework. Tests on 220 graphs show competitive performance with MADAM using only triangle cuts. Together, these applications illustrate the representation's usefulness as a building block for first-order methods.
tldr: The paper introduces a box-cone representation of bound-factor RLT constraints for semidefinite relaxations of binary quadratic programs, enabling efficient first-order (ADMM) solution methods.
motivation: Linear inequalities multiplied by binary variables generate very large constraint systems in SDP relaxations, making the quadratic subproblems of splitting methods expensive to solve.
method: All products generated from a single inequality are shown to share a common slack and to admit an exact representation in the standard cone over the unit box, letting inequalities be processed via independent explicit projections within a two-block ADMM scheme with reusable factorizations.
result: Experiments on 257 binary quadratic programs against SDPNAL+ and on 220 graphs for Max-Cut with triangle inequalities grouped into box cones show competitive performance with MADAM using only triangle cuts.
conclusion: The box-cone representation is a practical building block for first-order methods in SDP relaxations, avoiding enlargement of the semidefinite matrix and per-inequality slack variables.

title: Strong Law Of Large Numbers For Random Semigroups In Norm Topology
authors: A. E. Komagorov
abstract: ArXiv:2610.41346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies the strong law of large numbers for products of random uniformly continuous semigroups in Banach spaces. We propose a novel approach by treating the product of semigroups as a solution to an integral equation and establish a version of the SLLN in norm topology for arbitrary Banach spaces.
tldr: The paper proves a strong law of large numbers in norm topology for products of random uniformly continuous semigroups acting on arbitrary Banach spaces.
motivation: Products of random semigroups arise in the study of stochastic evolutions and random dynamical systems, but a law-of-large-numbers result in norm topology for general Banach spaces was lacking.
method: The product of semigroups is recast as the solution of an integral equation, which is then analyzed to extract the asymptotic almost-sure behavior of the normalized product.
result: A version of the strong law of large numbers is established in the norm topology, valid for arbitrary Banach spaces, extending previous results that required stronger hypotheses or more restricted settings.
conclusion: The integral-equation viewpoint provides a flexible route to strong convergence for random semigroup products, with potential applications to stochastic partial differential equations and random evolution equations.

title: Leo Constellation Analysis For Satellite IoT: An Analysis Of Coverage Gaps And Retransmissions
authors: Lowie Rombouts, Jeroen Famaey, Roger Sanchez-Vital
abstract: ArXiv:2610.41440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) constellations are a promising way to connect Internet of Things (IoT) devices beyond terrestrial coverage, yet the intermittent visibility of their satellites imposes hard constraints on system and protocol design. Coverage probability and other snapshot statistics, which are often computed without accounting for the terminal's latitude, are insufficient for this purpose. Designers also need the temporal structure of coverage: the rate of coverage gaps, their duration distribution and mean, and quantities such as the probability that a retransmission succeeds after an initial transmission has failed. We develop an ergodic framework for Walker Star constellations in which these quantities reduce to spatial integrals over a two-dimensional torus that can be evaluated efficiently. We validate the framework against a seven-day Simplified General Perturbations 4 (SGP4) simulation of the Iridium NEXT constellation and find close agreement for the coverage probability, the revisit-time distribution, and the retransmission success probability. A comparison of Walker Star configurations further shows that constellations with similar satellite counts can yield substantially different packet-delivery probabilities with at most one retransmission, depending on the number of orbital planes. The results show that the ergodic model accurately gives the long-run values that finite time-domain simulations can only approximate, providing researchers with a tractable basis for the analytical modelling of IoT connectivity over non-terrestrial networks (NTN).
tldr: An ergodic analytical framework for Walker Star LEO constellations that computes coverage-gap statistics and retransmission success probabilities for satellite IoT connectivity.
motivation: Snapshot coverage statistics neglect latitude dependence and the temporal structure of coverage (gap rates, gap-duration distributions, retransmission success), which are essential for designing IoT protocols over non-terrestrial networks.
method: The authors formulate an ergodic model in which coverage-gap and revisit-time quantities reduce to spatial integrals over a two-dimensional torus, and validate it against a seven-day SGP4 simulation of the Iridium NEXT constellation.
result: The model agrees closely with simulation for coverage probability, revisit-time distribution and single-retransmission success probability, and reveals that constellations with comparable satellite counts but different numbers of orbital planes can differ substantially in packet-delivery probability.
conclusion: The ergodic framework provides a tractable analytical basis for modelling IoT connectivity over LEO non-terrestrial networks, yielding long-run values that finite time-domain simulations only approximate.

title: Restricted Peirce's Law And Natural Deduction
authors: Satoru Niki
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The constructive logic JP' is known to be the weakest logic between intuitionistic and minimal logic that satisfies Glivenko's theorem. In spite of this natural and desirable formal property, the motivation for its notion of negation remains rather elusive: it can be characterised by a restriction of Peirce's law or by the double negation of ex falso quodlibet, neither of which is very intuitive. In order to have an alternative perspective on this negation, we study in this paper a couple of natural deduction systems for JP'. We first present a system that is normalisable and satisfies a restricted form of the subformula property. Then a modification of this system is introduced, whose rules satisfy the separation of connectives and the full subformula property. Afterwards we turn our attention to a typed lambda-calculus, with respect to which our natural deduction enjoys the Curry-Howard correspondence, followed by a concluding discussion.
tldr: The paper develops natural deduction systems and a typed lambda-calculus for the intermediate constructive logic JP', which sits between intuitionistic and minimal logic and satisfies Glivenko's theorem.
motivation: JP' is characterized by a restriction of Peirce's law or by double negation of ex falso quodlibet, but the intuitive meaning of its negation remains obscure, so the author seeks an alternative proof-theoretic perspective.
method: Two natural deduction systems are presented: one normalisable with a restricted subformula property, and a modified version whose rules satisfy separation of connectives and the full subformula property; a Curry-Howard-corresponding typed lambda-calculus is then formulated.
result: Both systems are shown to be adequate for JP', with normalization and (restricted or full) subformula properties established, and the lambda-calculus is shown to correspond to the natural deduction via Curry-Howard.
conclusion: The proof-theoretic and computational accounts clarify the non-classical negation of JP' and provide a more intuitive foundation for this intermediate logic.

title: How A Group That Cannot Communicate Knows Itself By Its Enemy
authors: Gregory Falco
abstract: ArXiv:2610.40835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Teams that cannot communicate seem stuck with what each member sees. We show that their opponent can tell them the rest. Silent hunters, jammed robots and traders who never meet all face an adversary that reacts to the group as a whole; every member can read that reaction, a tell, and learn what no member knows alone. One tell can do the work of a message from every member. The adversary would rather hide, but hiding interferes with its own task, and a team that commits in advance to how it will respond decides how much hiding is worth. A committed team never loses when its opponent cares more about its own goals, and does as well as a fully informed team exactly when the opponent's stake outweighs any gain from lying. Below that point the team learns more by trusting less: in a solved Gaussian model it obtains the truth by promising not to use all of it and keeps the cost the opponent would have paid to conceal; an exact test decides when this holds in finite games. How a team spreads its trust matters too. A lone uninformed member with a full-support prior needs a private coin, but with additive squared-error losses two interchangeable members who respond differently replace it, and a small discount on trust insures against misjudging the enemy. Information, on this view, is not only gathered or aggregated; it is produced by how a team commits to respond.
tldr: A game-theoretic account of how teams of non-communicating agents can learn about the world by reading an adversary's reactive 'tells', showing when a pre-committed response strategy extracts information as effectively as full communication.
motivation: Teams whose members cannot communicate (silent hunters, jammed robots, traders who never meet) appear limited to local observations, yet an adversary reacting to the group as a whole leaks global information that each member can observe.
